result: A feedforward transthalamic pathway exists from M1L5 through motor thalamus to M2. The authors used optogenetics and retrograde tracing to demonstrate that M1L5 inputs drive M2-projecting neurons in VA/VL motor thalamus, with 4 out of 25 fluororuby-positive cells showing photostimulation-dependent excitatory responses.
evaluation: Claims C8, C25, C63, and C96 collectively demonstrate the presence of a feedforward transthalamic pathway. The experimental design (retrograde labeling from M2, recording from labeled VA/VL neurons, optogenetic stimulation of M1L5) is appropriate and the data in Figure 1 provide direct evidence. However, the low success rate (4/25 cells, 16%) raises questions about the prevalence of this pathway, which the authors acknowledge may be underestimated due to technical limitations (C70-C73).

result: M1L5 terminals overlap with GABAergic inputs from both GPi and SNr in motor thalamus. Quantitative analysis shows approximately 10% overlap between M1L5 and GPi terminal zones, and 10-20% overlap between Cb and GPi terminals. SNr terminals show substantial overlap with M1L5 but little overlap with Cb.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C29-C30, and C38-C39 are supported by tricolor anterograde labeling experiments (Figures 2 and 4) with quantitative analysis. The methodology for quantifying overlap is described and appears sound, using thresholded fluorescence images and pixel counting. The findings challenge prior views of complete segregation (C4, C22, C28) and provide anatomical basis for functional convergence.

result: GABAergic inputs from GPi converge with excitatory M1L5 inputs onto single motor thalamic neurons. Of 42 cells receiving at least one input, 23.8% (10/42) received convergent input from both GPi and M1L5, while 76.2% received only one input.
evaluation: Claims C5, C31-C33, and C105 are supported by dual optogenetic experiments with appropriate controls (Figure 3). The authors used voltage clamp at different holding potentials to distinguish EPSCs from IPSCs, and pharmacologically confirmed the identity of inputs with gabazine and DNQX/AP5. The spatial distribution of convergent cells (C33) matches anatomical predictions from Figure 2. The proportion of convergent cells is substantial but not universal, consistent with the anatomical overlap data.

result: GABAergic GPi inputs converge with excitatory cerebellar inputs onto single motor thalamic neurons. Of 43 cells receiving at least one input, 37.2% (16/43) received convergent input from both GPi and Cb, challenging the traditional view of complete segregation.
evaluation: Claims C6, C35-C37 are supported by dual optogenetic experiments (Figure 3H-J). This finding is particularly significant as it contradicts the prevalent notion of functional segregation between cerebellar and basal ganglia inputs (C4, C22). The higher proportion of convergence (37.2%) compared to GPi-M1L5 convergence (23.8%) is consistent with the anatomical overlap data. The experimental approach and controls are appropriate.

result: SNr inputs converge with both M1L5 and cerebellar inputs onto single motor thalamic neurons. In the M1L5-SNr overlap zone, 26.3% (5/19) of cells received convergent input, with 45.5% of M1L5-receiving cells also receiving SNr input. In the Cb-SNr overlap zone, 31.6% (6/19) of cells received convergent input.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43 are supported by dual optogenetic experiments (Figure 5). The convergence of SNr with both M1L5 and Cb inputs extends the findings from GPi experiments. The interpretation in C43 that sparse anatomical overlap is sufficient for functional convergence is reasonable given the data. The experimental design and controls are appropriate, though sample sizes are modest (19 cells per experiment).

result: Both M1L5 and cerebellar inputs to motor thalamus have driver-type synaptic properties, characterized by paired-pulse depression, insensitivity to mGluR antagonists, and complete blockade by iGluR antagonists.
evaluation: Claims C53-C56, C80, C84, and C89 are supported by electrophysiological characterization (Figure 6). The authors used appropriate criteria to distinguish drivers from modulators (C44-C51) and tested responses at multiple frequencies (10 Hz and 40 Hz). The distal axon stimulation approach (>300 μm from recorded cell) is appropriate for reliable paired-pulse measurements. This resolves prior conflicting evidence (C52) about the nature of these inputs.

result: GPi inputs to motor thalamus show paired-pulse depression at both low and high frequencies, are unchanged by GABAB blockade, and are completely abolished by gabazine, indicating they do not activate GABAB receptors.
evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 6C). The characterization of GPi synaptic properties is thorough, testing responses at multiple frequencies and with appropriate pharmacological controls. The conclusion that GPi inputs do not activate GABAB receptors is appropriately qualified to the population of cells tested.

result: Cerebellar terminal size distribution and average size are the same within and outside the GPi overlap zone (2.53 ± 0.1 vs. 3.03 ± 0.3 μm², p=0.222), but terminal density is significantly lower within the GPi overlap zone (223.1 ± 37.4 vs. 458.8 ± 88.0 terminals, p=0.0317).
evaluation: Claims C59-C61, C87-C88 are supported by quantitative confocal microscopy analysis (Figure 7). The methodology for terminal size analysis is described in detail and appears sound. The finding that terminal size does not differ between zones supports the functional evidence that all Cb inputs are drivers (C62, C89). The statistical analysis is appropriate (Mann-Whitney U-test), though the sample size is modest (n=5 mice).

result: The basal ganglia can gate the thalamic transmission of M1L5 and cerebellar information to cortex. When basal ganglia outputs are active, they inhibit thalamic relays involved in transthalamic information transfer; when disinhibited, transthalamic transmission flows.
evaluation: Claims C7, C21, C90-C91, C93, C97-C98, C100, and C102 represent interpretations and speculations based on the convergence data. While the anatomical and functional convergence is well-demonstrated, the actual gating function has not been tested in intact animals. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation (C104, C113-C115), stating that additional experiments in intact animals are required. The interpretation is plausible and well-reasoned, but remains speculative without behavioral or in vivo functional evidence.

result: M1L5 neurons can affect motor thalamic activity through both an indirect disinhibitory pathway (via the basal ganglia loop) and a direct excitatory projection, as M1L5 axonal branches bypass the basal ganglia and most thalamic-projecting M1L5 neurons also branch to innervate the caudoputamen.
evaluation: Claims C106-C110 represent an interpretation based on the current study's demonstration of direct M1L5-to-thalamus projections combined with prior anatomical data (C109, citations to Economo et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2020). While the direct projection is demonstrated here, the dual control mechanism remains speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge that the precise organization (whether a single M1L5 neuron can target an individual thalamic relay through both pathways) is unknown (C112).

result: Only a subset of thalamic neurons receives convergent input from basal ganglia and M1L5 or Cb. The study's experimental design (focusing on M1 injections, incomplete ChR2 transfection, especially in Rbp4 mice where many L5 neurons do not express Cre) likely underestimates the actual proportion of convergent cells.
evaluation: Claims C68-C73 represent appropriate caveats and limitations of the study. The authors acknowledge that triple convergence has not been demonstrated functionally (C69), that only a subset of cells shows convergence (C70), and provide reasonable explanations for potential false negatives (C71-C73). These limitations are important for interpreting the quantitative convergence data and are appropriately discussed.

result: Prior work established that cerebellar afferents provide driving input to motor thalamus, VA/VL nuclei receive L5 inputs and project to motor preparatory regions, transthalamic pathways exist in sensory systems, and basal ganglia outputs (GPi and SNr) project to VA/VL. However, it remained unclear whether transthalamic pathways operate in the motor system, and cerebellar and basal ganglia inputs were thought to be segregated.
evaluation: Claims C9-C20, C22-C23, C26-C28 represent background knowledge and prior work that is appropriately cited. These claims establish the context and knowledge gaps that the current study addresses. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization of prior understanding is accurate.

result: Glutamatergic synapses are classified as drivers (primary information source, larger EPSPs, paired-pulse depression, no mGluR activation) or modulators (modify information reception, smaller EPSPs, paired-pulse facilitation, mGluR activation). Driver inputs represent the main information to be relayed to cortex, and identifying L5 as the driver input to many thalamic regions clarified transthalamic relay function.
evaluation: Claims C44-C51, C66-C67, C74-C77 represent established knowledge about synaptic classification and thalamic function, appropriately cited to Sherman and colleagues' prior work. This framework is essential for interpreting the current study's characterization of M1L5 and Cb inputs as drivers.

result: Prior studies showed conflicting evidence about M1L5 and Cb terminal properties in motor thalamus. The current study finds M1L5 inputs display driver characteristics but with smaller EPSC amplitudes than Cb inputs, potentially due to differences in convergence patterns. Driver synapses can occur from terminals of various sizes.
evaluation: Claims C78-C79, C81-C83, C85-C86 appropriately contextualize the current findings within prior conflicting literature. The interpretation that differences in EPSC amplitude may reflect convergence patterns (C82) is speculative but reasonable. The agreement with recent work (C85, Gornati et al., 2018) and the principle that driver synapses span a range of sizes (C86) are appropriately cited.

result: The traditional view situates basal ganglia within a cortex-basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex loop. Motor and frontal cortices are major sources of inputs to and targets of motor thalamic relays, with connections that can be reciprocal or non-reciprocal. Cortical areas have both direct and transthalamic connections organized in parallel. Similar organization has been anticipated in songbirds.
evaluation: Claims C92, C94-C95, C99, C101, C103, and C111 represent established knowledge and theoretical frameworks appropriately cited. These provide context for interpreting how the current findings extend or challenge traditional views of basal ganglia function.

result: Both GPi and SNr efferents converge with M1L5 or Cb inputs onto single motor thalamic neurons, which is different from previous demonstrations of Cb convergence with modulatory L6 inputs, as L5 projections are more selective and are drivers.
evaluation: Claims C64-C65 summarize key findings and appropriately distinguish them from prior work (Schäfer et al., 2021). The distinction between L5 (selective, driver) and L6 (ubiquitous, modulator) convergence is important for interpreting the functional significance of the findings.

result: Future work is needed to test the gating hypothesis through causal behavioral experiments in intact animals and to investigate whether inhibitory gating of transthalamic pathways occurs across higher order thalamic nuclei.
evaluation: Claims C104, C113-C115 appropriately outline necessary future experiments to test the study's interpretations and extend the findings. These represent reasonable next steps given the current data.
